data.title: Cypress Creek Restoration Project — Urban Salmon Habitat Recovery in West Vancouver
data.primary_action: Urban stream habitat restoration and salmon recovery
data.secondary_action: Riparian zone stabilization and community-based watershed stewardship
data.support_needed:
Support for:
•	Continued riparian restoration and invasive species removal
•	Native vegetation replanting
•	Monitoring and habitat assessment
•	Community engagement and youth stewardship programs
•	Educational outreach and watershed awareness
data.problem_statement:
Urbanization, altered water flow, invasive species, and historical channel modification have degraded sections of Cypress Creek, reducing spawning habitat quality for salmon and other native species. Climate change further stresses freshwater systems through increased storm intensity and temperature shifts.

Without active restoration and stewardship, urban salmon populations risk further decline.
data.result_and_outcome:
•	Improved spawning habitat conditions in Cypress Creek
	•	Increased native riparian vegetation coverage
	•	Strengthened local salmon recovery efforts
	•	Enhanced community awareness of urban watershed protection
	•	Long-term stewardship model established for continued habitat protection
data.description_of_solution:
The Cypress Creek Restoration Project focuses on restoring ecological function within an urban watershed.

By stabilizing streambanks, re-establishing native riparian vegetation, and improving habitat complexity, the project enhances spawning and rearing conditions for salmon and other native freshwater species. Community involvement ensures sustained stewardship and long-term monitoring.

The approach integrates habitat restoration with public engagement, building resilience within a highly developed coastal ecosystem.
data.org_mission: The Cypress Creek Restoration Project supports long-term salmon recovery and freshwater ecosystem resilience through community-led habitat restoration and stewardship in West Vancouver.
data.activities:
•	Removal of invasive plant species
•	Replanting native riparian vegetation
•	Streambank stabilization
•	Ongoing watershed monitoring
•	Volunteer coordination and stewardship days
•	Collaboration with local environmental commission and streamkeepers
data.impact_tracks:
Urban Habitat Restoration
Improves spawning and rearing habitat for salmon within an urbanized watershed.

Salmon Recovery
Supports the return and long-term viability of Pacific salmon species in Cypress Creek.

Riparian Ecosystem Rehabilitation
Stabilizes streambanks, improves water quality, and restores native vegetation.

Community Stewardship
Engages local volunteers, environmental commission members, and youth in hands-on watershed protection.

Climate Resilience
Strengthens natural flood buffering and freshwater ecosystem health in the face of increasing climate volatility.
data.species_focus: Coho salmon, Chum salmon, Cutthroat trout, riparian bird species, amphibians, freshwater invertebrates
data.impact_numbers:
•	Restoration work within Cypress Creek watershed in West Vancouver
	•	Improved habitat for:
	•	Coho salmon
	•	Chum salmon
	•	Coastal cutthroat trout
	•	Removal of invasive species in riparian zones
	•	Replanting of native vegetation to stabilize streambanks
	•	Ongoing volunteer stewardship hours contributing to watershed protection
	•	Protection of critical urban freshwater habitat connected to Howe Sound ecosystem
	•	Supports annual enhancement of approximately 3,000 Coho salmon, with 10,000 Coho released in the most recent year
data.lessons_learned:
Urban streams can recover when consistent stewardship is applied.
	•	Salmon habitat protection requires long-term monitoring, not one-time intervention.
	•	Riparian vegetation restoration is foundational to water temperature regulation and spawning success.
	•	Community engagement increases long-term protection outcomes.
	•	Small urban creeks are critical ecological arteries, not marginal systems.

data.title: Empowered Filmmaker — Indigenous Cultural Preservation, Governance & Environmental Storytelling Initiative
data.primary_action: Community-based capacity building for Indigenous habitat protection
data.secondary_action: Documentation of salmon stewardship, wildlife corridors, and Indigenous Protected Areas
data.support_needed:
•	Expansion into additional Indigenous communities
	•	Professional equipment grants for habitat documentation
	•	Youth and Elder mentorship in ecological storytelling
	•	Travel and delivery costs for community-based programs
	•	Long-term distribution and impact campaigns focused on conservation outcomes
data.problem_statement:
Many Indigenous territories facing habitat threats lack access to professional storytelling tools necessary to influence environmental policy and public discourse. While salmon systems, wildlife corridors, and freshwater ecosystems are under increasing pressure from industrial development and climate change, communities often lack media infrastructure to document impacts and assert governance authority.

Without internal storytelling capacity, conservation narratives risk being externally controlled and disconnected from Indigenous ecological law.
data.result_and_outcome:
•	645+ Indigenous filmmakers trained to document habitat protection
	•	214+ conservation-related films produced
	•	Strengthened documentation of salmon systems, watersheds, and wildlife corridors
	•	Increased youth participation in habitat stewardship narratives
	•	Expanded Indigenous-led conservation advocacy across participating regions
	•	Long-term storytelling infrastructure established in multiple communities
data.description_of_solution:
Empowered Filmmaker builds conservation capacity from within Indigenous communities.

Rather than positioning habitat protection as an external intervention, the program equips local storytellers to document salmon restoration, land-use challenges, climate impacts, and Indigenous Protected Areas using professional media tools.

By combining technical filmmaking excellence with traditional ecological knowledge, the initiative strengthens Indigenous-led habitat protection efforts and supports long-term environmental governance.
data.org_mission: Empowered Filmmaker strengthens Indigenous-led habitat protection by transferring professional storytelling skills directly to communities. The program equips participants to document salmon stewardship, watershed protection, wildlife corridors, and Indigenous Protected Areas while preserving cultural and ecological knowledge systems.
data.activities:
•	Delivered immersive filmmaking intensives focused on conservation storytelling
	•	Provided professional cameras, drones, audio equipment, and editing training
	•	Mentored participants from concept to final conservation-focused film
	•	Facilitated community screenings to support habitat protection awareness
	•	Supported distribution to festivals, broadcasters, and online platforms
	•	Provided ongoing mentorship and equipment access
data.impact_tracks:
Habitat Protection Capacity Building
Trains Indigenous community members to document and advocate for salmon habitat, wildlife corridors, watershed protection, and Indigenous Protected Areas.

Indigenous Protected Areas Support
Participant films contribute to visibility and legitimacy of Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs).

Watershed & Salmon Stewardship
Supports storytelling around restoration, climate resilience, and freshwater protection within the Skeena and other northern watersheds.

Intergenerational Ecological Knowledge Transfer
Documents traditional ecological knowledge that underpins long-term habitat stewardship.

Community-Led Conservation
Builds internal media capacity so conservation narratives are Indigenous-led rather than externally framed.
data.species_focus: Pacific salmon (5 species), caribou, grizzly bear, moose, freshwater ecosystems, old-growth forests (varies by community)
data.impact_numbers:
•	645+ Indigenous filmmakers trained
	•	214+ Indigenous-made films produced
	•	Films addressing:
	•	Salmon habitat protection
	•	Indigenous Protected Areas
	•	Mineral tenure and watershed impacts
	•	Wildfire stewardship
	•	Land-use and territorial governance
	•	Programs delivered across multiple Indigenous territories in BC and Alberta
	•	148,000+ hours of hands-on conservation storytelling training
	•	Millions of cumulative views and community screenings
	•	Long-term equipment access and mentorship provided to graduates
data.lessons_learned:
•	Habitat protection is strongest when communities control their own narratives.
	•	Indigenous law and ecological knowledge are foundational to long-term conservation success.
	•	Youth engagement strengthens intergenerational habitat stewardship.
	•	Professional storytelling tools significantly increase policy influence and public credibility.
	•	Cultural preservation and habitat protection are inseparable in Indigenous contexts.

data.title: HA NII TOKXW: Our Food Table — Advancing the Meziadin Indigenous Protected Area
data.primary_action: Indigenous Protected Area establishment through hereditary law governance
data.secondary_action: Salmon habitat protection and wildlife corridor preservation
data.support_needed: Support for strategic distribution, policy engagement, and scaling Indigenous-led storytelling tied to Indigenous Protected Areas. Additional funding will expand impact campaigns and governance-based conservation documentation.
data.problem_statement: Colonial policies fragmented Gitanyow territory through the reserve system and residential schools, disrupting governance transmission and food sovereignty. Industrial pressures threatened salmon-bearing waters and wildlife corridors within the Skeena watershed. Despite BC’s DRIPA legislation, meaningful UNDRIP implementation requires visible recognition of Indigenous law in land governance.
data.result_and_outcome:
•	Advancement of the Meziadin Indigenous Protected Area
	•	Protection of salmon habitat and wildlife corridors
	•	Strengthened recognition of hereditary law in land-use discussions
	•	International awareness through 21,600+ screenings
	•	Practical example of UNDRIP implementation under BC’s DRIPA framework
data.description_of_solution: The film reframed conservation as Indigenous jurisdiction rather than external environmental protection. By documenting Gitanyow hereditary law, salmon stewardship, and territorial responsibility, it translated Indigenous governance into a format accessible to policymakers and global audiences. This strengthened recognition of Gitanyow authority and supported advancement of the Meziadin Indigenous Protected Area (~55,000 hectares).
data.org_mission: VoVo Productions creates award-winning films that protect critical ecosystems and advance Indigenous sovereignty through powerful storytelling. We support Indigenous nations in documenting hereditary governance systems, strengthening territorial stewardship, and accelerating meaningful implementation of UNDRIP.
data.activities:
•	Produced and directed HA NII TOKXW in collaboration with the Gitanyow Hereditary Chiefs
	•	Documented colonial history and residential school impacts
	•	Centered Gitanyow Ayookxw (hereditary law) as a living governance system
	•	Amplified salmon stewardship and wildlife protection practices
	•	Leveraged international awards and screenings to elevate governance visibility
data.impact_tracks:
Indigenous Sovereignty & Governance
The film strengthened recognition of Gitanyow hereditary law (Ayookxw) and supported advancement of the Meziadin Indigenous Protected Area under Indigenous jurisdiction.

UNDRIP / DRIPA Implementation
Provided a practical example of Indigenous law being exercised in land-use governance aligned with British Columbia’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (2019).

Habitat & Biodiversity Protection
Contributed to protection of approximately 55,000 hectares (550 km²) within the Meziadin watershed, part of the globally significant Skeena River system.

Food Sovereignty & Cultural Continuity
Documented salmon stewardship systems sustaining both biodiversity and Gitanyow food security.

Policy & Public Awareness
Elevated hereditary governance internationally through screenings, awards, and policy engagement.
data.species_focus: acific salmon (Chinook, Sockeye, Coho, Pink, Chum), Grizzly bear, Moose, Mountain goat, Wolf, Wolverine, Skeena watershed biodiversity
data.impact_numbers:
•	~55,000 hectares (550 km²) protected within the Meziadin Indigenous Protected Area
	•	Protection of habitat supporting:
	•	5 species of Pacific salmon
	•	Grizzly bear populations
	•	Moose, mountain goat, wolf, wolverine
	•	30+ mammal species
	•	100+ bird species
	•	Meziadin watershed connected to the Skeena River — one of the largest wild salmon systems on Earth
	•	21,600+ documented screenings and international viewings
	•	Contributed to conservation aligned with Canada’s 30x30 biodiversity commitments
data.lessons_learned:
•	Indigenous law is a durable conservation model when publicly asserted and documented.
	•	Colonial disruption weakened governance visibility but did not eliminate hereditary authority.
	•	UNDRIP implementation requires practical, territorial examples — not just legislation.
	•	Conservation rooted in food sovereignty is more sustainable than externally imposed protection models.
	•	International recognition strengthens local negotiating power.

data.title: Cultural Ecotones in Mallorca
data.support_needed: Financial
data.problem_statement: The island of Mallorca in Spain is a highly popular tourist destination with rising tension between locals and foreigners causing an expanding rift in culture and resulting in decreasing planetary health. What are the underlying beliefs and values driving people apart and what might reconcile them?
data.result_and_outcome:
Our ultimate goal is shifting culture in a way that births new stakeholder guilds of diverse stakeholders from where planetary health initiatives will grow regeneratively.
350+ people will be directly involved over the course of the year, with the intention of growing the circles. 
At the end of our first year, we will have an exhibition, a printed publication, and an online presence, all conveying our results, our methodology, and process including what elements worked and what didn't, stakeholders involved, key findings, synthesised learnings, identified diverging perspectives and articulated reconciling field, potential and projected next steps.

We will utilise artistic skills to a high degree to augment and visualise learnings in an engaging, conscious evolving and transparent way during the process and in our final output. 

Culture change is a soft concept and measured indirectly. We will observe, track and document any shifts in values, beliefs, and behaviours. We will measure the number of people involved, publicise qualitative statements and knowledge, the steps in our process, research questions asked, frameworks and methodologies applied, how we formed our synthesis, what budding interventions are emerging within groups, and more. It is a blend of academia, design, and regenerative practices which in itself is a new and measurable result. 
 
Hopefully the circles will be the beginning of things to manifest in the future where also quantitative data can be measured.
data.description_of_solution: In 2026 we start working with the root of the cultural differences. We will host a series of gatherings for Mallorquins and foreign residents with themes that are interconnected parts of human culture and how they relate to their natural surroundings in Mallorca. The themes represent diverging interests which will serve as explorations for reconciliation and potential common ground. The circles serve to lay the groundwork for transforming culture as well as generating diverse stakeholder guilds of people interested in evolving beliefs and values held on the island.
data.org_mission: Our aim is to create cultural cohesion in a place of fragmentation and illustrate the path to accomplish it. We will create 'reconciling fields of caring', a term from Regenerative Design and Development, and demonstrate the role of the arts in changing our relationship with place and the natural world.
data.activities: Design Research. Two-Eyed circle gatherings. Art pop-ups, publications, and exhibitions. Co-creative sessions. Un-conference. Regenerative Design and Development.
data.impact_tracks: Document project outcomes, potential shifts in beliefs and values,  and long-term effects of culture change on planetary health.
data.impact_numbers: 350 people participating in shifting culture towards planetary health focus and regenerative practices.
data.lessons_learned: to come

data.title: mbora - Affordable Microfinancing for Rural Farmers: Driving Nature-
data.primary_action: Reduced poaching by providing poachers with alternative livelihoods
data.secondary_action: Enhanced biodiversity by supporting smallholders to farm regeneratively for guaranteed markets
data.support_needed: Funding for working capital to put into microloans for farmers and village businesses; funding to establish a network of 3 x mbora Hubs around Nyika and Vwaza National Parks; funding to evolve mboraMAX the digital platform to improve digital access to financial services, healthcare, and educational content.
data.problem_statement:
Economic Inequality: Limited access to affordable credit stifles growth. Farmers and small businesses lack working capital, preventing investment in productive assets & improved agri techniques.
Environmental Degradation: Population pressure and poverty drive poaching & unsustainable practices. Deforestation for farmland and firewood, coupled with poor agricultural methods, leads to biodiversity loss, soil degradation, reduced yields, and increased vulnerability to climate shocks.
Healthcare Disparities: Long distances to clinics and unaffordable poor-quality care. Poor health outcomes hinder productivity, creating a cycle where illness reduces earning capacity and poverty limits access to healthcare.
Result: These challenges reinforce each other, creating a poverty trap where environmental degradation reduces agricultural productivity, poor health limits earning potential, and lack of financial resources prevents investment in sustainable solutions. This perpetuates inequality in underserved rural areas.
data.result_and_outcome:
Economic Outcomes (5 year time horizon):

- Approximately 83,000 new beneficiaries realised from households accessing services from mbora Hubs (based on current hub performance)
- Creation of sustainable livelihoods for ~7,500 outgrower farmers
- Estimated $600,000+ in annual farmer income from cash crops 
- Reduction in poaching pressure through alternative income generation
- New market access and trade routes for the region
- Strengthened local economy through increased circulation of capital
- Estimated 60+ direct jobs created at the mbora Hubs

Social Outcomes:

- Enhanced access to essential healthcare services for ~40,000 people
- Increased women's economic empowerment (typically 60%+ of members are women)
- Improved household financial stability through savings and loans
- Better access to education through increased household income
- Strengthened community cohesion through village banking groups
- Reduced human-wildlife conflict through alternative livelihoods
- Skills development and capacity building in farming communities

Environmental Outcomes:

- Reduced pressure on wildlife and forest resources
- Implementation of climate-smart agricultural practices
- Soil conservation and improvement through regenerative farming
- Creation of buffer zones around protected areas
- Enhanced community stake in conservation
- Reduction in slash-and-burn agriculture
- Biodiversity protection through reduced encroachment and burning
data.org_mission: mbora drives social, environmental, and economic transformation in rural Africa by empowering farmers and village businesses with innovative digital solutions and sustainable market access
data.impact_tracks: Number of active loans; Repayment Rates; Enhanced earnings of farmers; Reduced incidences of poaching
data.impact_numbers: 10,000 villagers financially included; >95% repayment rates; Farmers to increase earnings by up to 10 times; Incidences of poaching to decrease by 50% after 4 years.
data.lessons_learned: To stop poaching you first need to offer communities viable sustainable improved alternative livelihood strategies

data.title: Compassion in Fashion: Annual Fur-Free Festival
data.support_needed:
The collaboration with End Pandemics will strengthen our network with countries in Asia, add to our reputation and ability to call on spokespeople to incorporate credible messages into our consumer education campaign. The collaboration will accelerate our aim to encourage positive and responsible consumer behaviour which will help to shape the values of business and industries from a view point of compassionate lifestyle; fur free and sustainable fashion and enable us to extend this avoiding pandemics in the future.
The consumer education campaign will be able to rally a strong following in China of millennial and Generation Z (the largest consumer group) who will in turn, become spokespeople and leaders of community change and action for issues relating to One Health.
data.problem_statement:
Indiscriminate consumption globally and in China is fueling unsustainable industries such as fur farming. In fur farming, disregard is shown for human welfare in terms of employment and safety, exploitation of animals and damage to the environment. The risks of pandemics is becoming clearer but when people are shopping there is a disconnect between individual actions and impacts to other people, animals and the environment. 
The legal trade in fur is a starting point to tackle the trade in wildlife and prevent future pandemics. At the same time as ACTAsia works for a reduction in demand for wildlife as a whole, we aim to build a consumer mind set, who understand compassionate choices and the destructive effects that over and indiscriminate consumption has on the world, from all of the One Health perspectives.
These choices such as fur in fashion fuel unsustainable industries and put human health at risk from toxic chemicals and the potential for pandemics. The risks of pandemics is becoming clearer but when people are shopping, there is a disconnect of the two issues. 
The legal trade in fur is a starting point to tackle the commercial trade in wildlife and prevent future pandemics. At the same time as ACTAsia works for a reduction in demand for wildlife as a whole, we aim to build a consumer mind set, of people who understand compassionate choices and the positive impacts they can have on the world, from a One Health perspective.
data.result_and_outcome:
ACTAsia has been delivering the Fashion Festival in China for six years and have built up to 2020 where we have made the event offline and online, had international speakers join from around the world online and in person, and been able to pull in brands for sustainable fashion and in 2020 started to broaden the reach to consumers of plant-based diet including OATLY. 
Held in China to include: Fashion Show, Forum and Fur-Free day.
Media pick up from 20 media agencies in China
Total reach for the event this year (2020) was close to 40 million people. 
In ACTAsia consumer report 2020 we have found that a higher percentage of fur consumers will stop buying fur once they know about the practices in fur farms and more about the industry. This has increased from 65% in 2019 to 84% in 2020. 
We measure success by the partnerships, strong political support, that the Fur-Free message is within the larger sustainability discussion and has become mainstream, this has been a crucial goal and one ACTAsia has been keen to work towards. ACTAsia has steadily built a robust and credible reputation in China and internationally through diligent research work and reporting on evidence and maintaining context and integrity within our work. We have honoured partners and given credit where it is due, delivering what we set out to achieve. 
Over the six years of Fashion Festivals we have hand-picked key speakers who we respect and know they have something key and individual to bring to the forums, we have showcased fur free brands and maintained a positive message on consumer choices. ACTAsia avoids the radical or bandwagon and does not use aggression or finger-pointing tactics. Instead we are non-confrontational, offering positive consumer choices and back up with the reasoning to explain and inform with benefits to people, animals and the environment. 
Through the media we have become a called upon source for accurate up to date information, this is due to the approach we have taken to ensure we research and fact check before sharing information with others. ACTAsia keeps the fur issue within mainstream media and have avoided being side-lined or tarnished as a ‘radical’ group that is then dismissed. 
Promoting open and honest discussion and not condemning but celebrating small changes, not driving for perfection in consumer choices but showing that small changes can add up makes people feel they are willing to join us.

data.title: Caring for Life education programme
data.support_needed: ACTAsia have a strategy for Caring for Life primary curriculum and the support from End Pandemics will accelerate the achievement of our targets and expand our reach to schools and countries in Asia.
data.problem_statement: ACTAsia are working to support the education systems in China and Asia where personal development or character education is lacking. Caring for Life curriculum for children works with teachers and education authorities to help to address several problems across society in China. The curriculum covers issues surrounding humans, animals and the environment and explores the interactions and impacts one has on the other, reinforcing the interconnectedness, along with an insight into humans effect on each other, animals and our planet through over use, intensive farming, pollution from factories and transport, resulting in climate change, loss of biodiversity and risk of disease including zoonosis. Children are encouraged to have their own voice to start clubs at schools for issues such as recycling, gardening and friendship. Recently children in China during lockdown joined in a CFL competition to create a poster to warn others of the dangers of eating wildlife and causing pandemics see Yuteng at this link https://www.actasia.org/news/wildlife-off-the-menu-for-yuteng-and-friends/
data.result_and_outcome: The programme has been established for 8 years in China and has so far reached 93,000 children through 148 schools and trained 3,100 teachers to deliver the curriculum. The education programme is evaluated for four attributes; prosocial behaviour, empathy, attitudes to animals and attitudes to the environment which show the impact of the curriculum: Nurturing Kindness Naturally Journal Paper was published in 2018 and explains how the evaluation was carried out and that the CFL curriculum leads to increased prosocial behaviour in children. Using the CHEAKS assessment scale – the Children’s Environmental Attitude and Knowledge Scale, the evaluation shows significant improvements in behaviours addressing environmental issues among children who participate in ACTAsia’s CFL curriculum. These positive changes include improved attitudes towards water, energy, animals and recycling. The most recent paper published in the International Journal for Humane Education is ‘A world of good’. There are two further journal papers for empathy and attitudes to animals in the pipeline. See appendices for papers. In July 2019, the Caring for Life curriculum has been recognised by the UN High Level Political Forum as meeting the following targets of Goal 4. Quality Education; 4.2, 4.7 and 4.A and also recognised that the following Goals are also involved; 10,12, 13, 14, 15 & 16.
data.description_of_solution: The Caring for Life curriculum was written within the guidelines of the UNESCO pillars of education in particular ‘Learning to live Together’. The education programme is central to changing hearts and minds and ensuring that students have the opportunity to think critically and analyse information, including cultural norms. Being able to make decisions with compassion in mind is vital to long-term behaviour change and the future of the planet will depend on it. The programme is delivered by qualified teachers within China and shortly in Pakistan and is embedded into the curriculum, and is delivered in a structured and planned manner with age relevance.  ACTAsia aim to keep a Pioneer Network of 10 schools which will receive the support of the team for teacher training and a grant to supply the necessary resources. This means close to 9,000 children will receive CFL in their academic year. Embedding the Caring for Life within the existing education system is key to being able to deliver a holistic curriculum taught by professional teachers to reach as many children and communities as possible.
data.org_mission: By educating children, consumers and professionals, ACTAsia promotes kindness and compassion for people, animals and the environment among Asian societies. We help people learn to care for all life at a time when global populations are growing, and our planet faces its severest challenges yet.
data.activities: ACTAsia’s mission is integral to the EndPandemics campaign. Targeting human behaviour change is key to ending pandemics for good in our lifetime. Education is key to long term human behaviour change and the Caring for Life education programme involves teachers, students, parents, families and communities. Our education programme is a professional primary curriculum which can be delivered in schools in Asia addressing the root causes of over consumption, commercial wildlife trade and destruction of the environment. The curriculum helps to develop key concepts including’ critical thinking, responsibility and emotional intelligence. The children who receive the curriculum today are the leaders and decision makers of the future.
data.impact_numbers: 11 Member groups initiated across Asia, 21 Plant based events including webinars and food-swap challenges, 17.1m+ Reached with plant-based messages
data.lessons_learned: ACTAsia has been delivering the Caring for Life curriculum in China since 2012. The programme started without government partnership and we realise now that this is a huge stumbling block for reaching our aim of incorporating the CFL curriculum into the national curriculum of the country. In our second country, Pakistan, the initial partnership is directly with government education authorities and a local NGO to help facilitate the aim. In China we are still gently lobbying for local education authorities to support the curriculum and it's concepts which we will keep pushing towards education bureaus and finally the central government. The scale of China means ACTAsia is unable to reach all children in the country and with several rural difficult to reach places this is made more challenging, we have learned to adapt to a digital platform, though this is not our full or best curriculum, it is something and reaches an additional 30,000 children in rural areas (in 2019) and we are learning that we need to improve this offer in the future. We have learned that the curriculum works best when delivered by professional teachers, rather than parents, but that parents can play a reinforcing role at home and as volunteers for summer camps. Advice for this programme is to evaluate from the start, budget and plan time for this (in our case an additional staff member), this is essential for to give credibility to the project, both for governments to see and funding organisations. Success should look like the Caring for Life curriculum adopted into the national curriculum so that every child (and teacher) in the country has the opportunity to develop critical thinking, emotional intelligence and make compassionate choices which will enable sustainable long-term behaviour change.

data.title: ADI's Operation Spirit of Freedom - Stop Circus Suffering campaign
data.support_needed: One message the current pandemic crisis has exposed is the critical need to work together, outside our respective silos, to honestly assess and address humans’ use and abuse of nature, among other inequities. Our health and the health of all who share this world with us demands that we restore balance to our planet's biodiversity and supporting habitat, and learn to coexist with its many species and critical ecosystems. The campaign's interdisciplinary approach and global reach offers diverse inputs and avenues to broaden and amplify this critical message.
data.problem_statement: Wildlife trade, trafficking, and exploitation causes unhealthy and inappropriate attitudes toward and relationships with animals, which harms individual animals, wild populations, ecosystems, and, as we now know all too well, human health.
data.result_and_outcome: In 2007, ADI began a 2-year undercover investigation in Latin America, which, among other things, led to Peru's 2011 ban on the use of wild animals in circuses and, ultimately, a nationwide trafficking enforcement effort led by the government. In the end, ADI rescued more than 115 wild animals from the circus industry, trafficking, and pet trade. This film clip features 39 primates rehomed to sanctuary habitats we constructed for them in the Amazon jungle, with several eligible for reintroduction to the wild (including a new baby who arrived during the process). Elsewhere, in the Peruvian cloud forests, ADI completed the nation's first Andean bear sanctuary, providing a home for 3 long-suffering bears, and opportunity for more rescues in future. ADI also worked with authorities to export nonnative animals (lions and tigers) to sanctuary outside the country, supporting their goal to distinguish what wild means in Peru, versus elsewhere, to manage public expectations and understanding of animals native to Peru. Success indicators included national legislation, supported by ongoing enforcement, and a shift in general public attitudes, no longer automatically accepting wildlife exploitation as appropriate or given. There's always more work to be done; however, the nationwide campaign to pull all animals trafficked at that moment in time, was a clear message to traffickers that laws will be enforced, there will be consequences, and animals will be confiscated.
data.description_of_solution: ADI's Operation Spirit of Freedom - related to wild animal trade and trafficking for pet trade and entertainment in Peru
data.org_mission: To educate, create awareness, and promote the interest of humanity in the cause of justice, and the suppression of all forms of cruelty to animals; wherever possible, to alleviate suffering, and to conserve and protect animals and their environment.
data.activities: ADI takes a holistic approach, working for long-term, meaningful change, to protect animals and their environment. ADI campaigns run the spectrum from start to finish - undercover investigations to reveal the reality; research to gather empirical evidence for scientific, economic and technical reports; public education and advocacy to change laws, attitudes, and behavior; and rescues to save those individuals left behind and to support law enforcement - to end animal exploitation, trade, and trafficking, toward justice for all species.
data.impact_tracks: Public Policies, Consumer Behaviors, Business Practices
data.impact_numbers: Nationwide ban on the use of wild animals in circuses as well as a local ban on all animals in Magdalena del Mar
data.lessons_learned: Comprehensive, country-wide campaigns are arduous, requiring steadfast  commitment as they ebb and flow in popular regard, and the flexibility to think on your feet as conditions change. Change is difficult, and governmental entities taking on complex and potentially controversial tasks were not sure how they might be received. In the end, its success, including its PR success, motivated ongoing action and a generally more empathetic view toward wild animals, who belong in the wild with their own kind. Thanks to a comprehensive campaign, combined with widespread public education and NGO support, authorities were ultimately encouraged by the public rally toward change for the better. They became the unexpected heroes in the story, as perceptions changed, newly questioning status quo exploitation of wild animals trafficked in their country, which inspired further action. Work remains to be done of course, as it always does, but we showed that it can be done, that it should be done.

data.title: Conservation Agreements: an opportunity for people of the forest

data.problem_statement: The premontane humid forests located on the border between Boyacá (Paya) and Casanare (Nunchia), in Colombia (5° 35.626'N, 72° 21.218'W), are one of the last remnants of primary forest in the region, harboring an important diversity of flora and fauna, among which is a new population of endangered spider monkey (Ateles belzebuth). Most forests are threatened by the expansion of the agricultural frontier. Every year the peasants slash and burn dozens of hectares to establish subsistence crops that after two years they will leave as paddocks for small-scale livestock. This practice, in addition to degrading the soil, reducing biodiversity, threatening their food security and increasing the vulnerability of the inhabitants of the area to extreme climatic events (torrential rains and droughts), also is creating new scenarios for the generation and propagation of future zoonotic diseases. In addition, the lack of institutional and governmental presence and the recent construction of an access road (in progress), become a new threat to the forest, since it can favor selective logging and hunting, especially during this time of COVID-19 quarantine, where there is even less presence of environmental authorities.

·     We have been working with 24 families in a PES strategy to preserve 400 ha of forest and to conserve a recently discovered Spider monkey (A. belzebuth) population (EN) during the last 3 years.
·      We have gain knowledge about Ateles belzebuth population size, density, food availability, types of fruit consumed, this is a basic information to develop the conservation strategy.
·      We have a deeper comprehension of the relationship of people with the forest, how they use the forest resources, in which quantities, activities, which species, how often, and the cultural bases behind it. This information is the base of the alternatives build with the communities for a better forest use and which will be consolidate at the conservation and production agreements.
 ·      We expect to establishment of conservation and production agreements with two rural communities who lived around the forest where A. belzebuth was found. With this agreements we want to promote better production practices, and constitute new areas of forest under conservation
data.description_of_solution: Reduce pressure on the forest and expand wildlife habitats, through Conservation and production agreements that offer sustainable production alternatives and environmentally-friendly livelihoods to the communities who depend on the forest.
data.org_mission: We are an NGO with the conviction that a strengthened environmental and democratic awareness can transform our relationship with the territory. In this sense, we promote the governance and conservation of territories through strategies that inspire and facilitate critical participation in their planning and use.

These CPA will allow the forest conservation to continue, offering productive alternatives that will improve the quality of life of the families involved and the inhabitants of the region and contribute to maintenance of the forest, wildlife habitats and environmental services.

data.title: Strengthening enforcement of wildlife laws
data.support_needed: We are a small Vietnamese non-governmental organization leading the fight against illegal wildlife trade, trafficking, and consumption. For more than 20 years, achievements to end Vietnam’s illegal wildlife trade have been possible thanks to donors who support creative, strategic, and decisive actions that protect wildlife in the short term and long term. Your support is crucial to continuing these efforts and safeguarding a sustainable future for wildlife, both in Vietnam and globally.
data.problem_statement: There are many wildlife trafficking networks run by Vietnamese nationals, regionally and globally, shipping tons of wildlife across continents, all destined for Vietnam and China. While this has been a continuing problem for many years, the current Covid-19 pandemic and its direct link to the wildlife trade demands a push for improved performance from local law enforcement agencies around the country to address wildlife crime, in order to bring the illegal wildlife trade in Vietnam to an end and thereby safeguard the future health of all people.
data.result_and_outcome: ENV’s efforts have made a significant impact on national wildlife policy that is critical for strengthening wildlife protection in Vietnam. This impact is a result of advocating favorable government decisions on major policy issues identified by ENV and establishing important precedents at the national and provincial levels.
data.description_of_solution: ENV has operated a national toll-free wildlife crime hotline since 2005. After receiving a public report, ENV works closely with law enforcement agencies to address the wildlife crime immediately, tracking each case through to conclusion and documenting the results on ENV’s secure, web-based Wildlife Crime Database. ENV has developed a comprehensive procedure for dealing with different types of wildlife crime. Depending on the crime, actions can range from warning letters sent to business owners, to working in collaboration with law enforcement agencies to arrest a serious offender. The core of ENV’s implemented solution lies in leveraging the risk of the Covid-19 pandemic to public health in these actions and communications, as well as in instances where authorities fail to respond adequately to shut down a restaurant selling wildlife or address other consumer-end crimes. The fact of the matter is that law enforcement agencies and officials have to now more than ever be pushed to do their jobs and bring the illegal wildlife trade in Vietnam to its knees, and that’s what ENV has been focusing on for the last few months.
data.org_mission: Education for Nature-Vietnam (ENV) focuses on combating the illegal wildlife trade in Vietnam through a combined strategy: strengthening law enforcement, improving legislation, and reducing consumer demand.
data.activities: ENV Wildlife Crime Unit (WCU) was created to support law enforcement authorities across Vietnam by alerting them to public reports of wildlife crime and assisting them in the legal procedures required to effectively combat wildlife crime, including dealing with confiscated wildlife and strictly punishing criminals. The WCU is composed of eight team members who work directly with the public and authorities across the country on a daily basis to tackle wildlife crime and uphold wildlife protection laws.
data.impact_numbers: 3,595 REPORTED CASES
data.lessons_learned: 1. The promotion of transparency in law enforcement is cardinal for the success of any cooperation between law enforcement and wildlife conservation organizations, as it creates accountability and establishes a foundation of mutual trust.

data.title: Legal advocacy and closing loopholes in wildlife law and policy
data.support_needed: We are a small Vietnamese non-governmental organization leading the fight against illegal wildlife trade, trafficking, and consumption. For more than 20 years, achievements to end Vietnam’s illegal wildlife trade have been possible thanks to donors who support creative, strategic, and decisive actions that protect wildlife in the short term and long term. Your support is crucial to continuing these efforts and safeguarding a sustainable future for wildlife, both in Vietnam and globally.
data.problem_statement: Current legislation allows for the mismanagement of commercial wildlife facilities and the indiscriminate establishment and registration of so-called “wildlife conservation” facilities in Vietnam, when in fact little to no conservation contributions are made by such facilities and their intended purpose is often only to serve as legal smokescreens for illegal wildlife laundering. These facilities are highly unsanitary environments where dead and dying animals are exposed to humans and each other, posing great health risks in terms of zoonotic diseases and cementing the need for a new law addressing the existing loopholes and tightening these facilities’ management. Along with these facilities, ENV has also identified restaurants, markets, and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) shops as other high-risk areas in terms of human contact with wildlife and potential exposure to zoonotic diseases.
data.result_and_outcome: Additionally, this ENV team works closely with court authorities across the country to promote the application of Penal Code 2015 (amended 2017) to prosecute wildlife criminals. As part of these efforts, ENV provides authorities with support during their investigation processes and assists them in the correct application of the law. When necessary, also ENV intervenes in the prosecution process to ensure local courts apply the law strictly and appropriately and criminals do not get away with their crimes.
data.description_of_solution: ENV has been using the Prime Minister’s Directive No. 29/CTT-TTg to encourage better enforcement of wildlife protection laws at the provincial level. Furthermore, a project with Vietnam’s Ministry of Health (MoH) is underway in which the MoH will issue instructions to all TCM practitioners around the country not to prescribe any medicine made from wildlife. The project also includes the production of a new guideline aimed at leveraging local law enforcement to address illegal wildlife trade operations that present potentially serious risk to public health such as wildlife farms, restaurants, markets, and TCM shops. These initiatives will be followed by massive media campaigns that will help amplify the message. Covid-19 messaging has also been included in all correspondence with law enforcement agencies and officers and justice system officials as leverage for strictly punishing wildlife crime in accordance with the law. Finally, taking the opportunity presented by Covid-19, ENV is working with the Ministry of Agricultural and Rural Development (MARD) to tighten up the management of wildlife facilities in Vietnam, as wildlife facilities can be classified as high-risk areas in terms of public health. This includes the development of a law to effectively manage wildlife facilities and placing greater responsibilities on local government and law enforcement authorities to eliminate wildlife laundering practices, thereby mitigating any threats to public health and safety due to unsound and illegal practices.
data.org_mission: Education for Nature-Vietnam (ENV) focuses on combating the illegal wildlife trade in Vietnam through a combined strategy: strengthening law enforcement, improving legislation, and reducing consumer demand.
data.activities: Currently, ENV is working with government ministries to formulate a law aimed at strengthening the effectiveness of management at Vietnamese wildlife facilities.
data.impact_numbers: 11,790 WILDLIFE VIOLATIONS ADDRESSED
data.lessons_learned:
1. It is important to identify the right contact person at an agency to ensure that the organization’s input is taken into account and included in the decision-making process. This contact also needs to be made in person, as well as through formal channels of correspondence to ensure success.
2. The use of a joint letter from NGOs was a successful way to highlight the issue and push along the Directive’s publication, illustrating the value of cooperative and interdisciplinary work among NGOs with similar goals.

data.title: Helping to reduce the demand and consumption of wildlife products through a public awareness and media campaign
data.support_needed: With the support of other organizations with similar goals, expertise and experiences can be shared to strengthen work done by all involved parties, ultimately creating a global effort to eradicate the illegal wildlife trade and make the world a safer place - both for humans and wildlife.
data.problem_statement: The problem is twofold. Firstly, while knowledge of the link between human contact with wildlife and zoonotic pandemics is becoming more prevalent, there are still members of Vietnamese society who need to be made aware of the fact. This in turn means that not everyone knows something like this is preventable – we can counteract any future outbreaks by breaking our links to wildlife. The illegal consumption, keeping, and trade of wild animals lies at the root of the problem, and by putting a stop to all such illegal activities, we can ensure the future safety and health of our communities. Secondly, this public awareness needs to stretch beyond the immediate state of panic created by Covid-19. People’s overall mindsets need to be changed to such an extent that emphasis remains on eradicating the illegal wildlife trade for the safety and health of our society – even after the current pandemic has been overcome.
data.result_and_outcome: Through free corporate partnerships with Goldsun Focus Media, Chicilon Media, and Saga Media, ENV’s Covid-19 campaign resources (various posters and the Covid-19 PSA) have been shared across Vietnam, with an estimated number of impressions of around 18 million across thousands of screens in residential and office buildings, airports, and public transport. The Covid-19 PSA has also been screened on more than 50 national TV channels, and various national TV news segments and national radio shows and ads have featured ENV’s Covid-19 content. Finally, through ongoing viral social media campaigns, ENV is reaching thousands of Vietnamese citizens on a weekly basis and engaging them with the Covid-19 messaging.
data.description_of_solution: Affecting behavioral change by raising public awareness on the link between the illegal wildlife trade and zoonotic pandemics, involving the public in ending the illegal wildlife trade, and impressing upon the Vietnamese government and enforcement agencies the grave importance of prohibiting the illegal wildlife trade on all fronts. This forms part of ENV’s integrated approach to combatting the illegal wildlife trade, made up of public awareness creation, enforcement, and legal advocacy, and these messages are delivered by ENV through various channels, including media statements to an extensive journalist network, viral social media campaigns, Public Service Announcement (PSA) films, radio shows and adverts on national radio, public events, and more. Alongside our efforts to educate the public and in order to effect greater change and achieve further reach, ENV expects the government to launch a national communication program designed to spread the message: Contact with wildlife directly threatens the health of our society.
data.org_mission: Education for Nature-Vietnam (ENV) focuses on combating the illegal wildlife trade in Vietnam through a combined strategy: strengthening law enforcement, improving legislation, and reducing consumer demand.
data.activities: Given the zoonotic nature of the current and the majority of past global pandemics, as well as Vietnam's status as a wildlife consumer country and go-between for the trade to other Southeast Asian countries, ENV's mission to end the illegal wildlife trade in and out of Vietnam helps to address one aspect of their root cause - humans' contact with and consumption of wildlife.
data.impact_numbers: 2,514 LIVE WILD ANIMALS CONFISCATED
data.lessons_learned:
1. It’s important to not only share media statements with our journalist network, but also to secure segments on TV and radio news programs to have a greater impact.
2. Resources need to be published in a timely manner, especially if they contain statistics that are time sensitive (e.g. Covid-19 statistics), to ensure the highest impact and most engagement from the public.
3. There is great value in securing partnerships with big media agencies for the purposes of reaching a wider audience, in ways that are not usually accessible to smaller NGOs.

data.title: Develop community level economic opportunities to deter local people from engaging in wildlife trafficking
data.support_needed: The idea is to show tourism agencies, operators, and hotels that small-scale nature tourism can be equally, if not more, lucrative than mass tourism, while enhancing awareness of the legal repercussions of profiting from the illegal use of wildlife in tourism.
data.problem_statement: Indigenous communities at the Colombian-Peruvian border are neglected by central governments who do not invest in the economic development of this region, leaving them with few options besides the unsustainable extraction of timber and wildlife to meet basic needs. The wild animals that supply the exotic pet trade, bushmeat trade, tourism, and biomedical research are sourced from indigenous territories with community members bearing the burden of carrying out the dangerous and illegal work of capturing and transporting poached animals for very little pay. Animals are stressed from capture in packed, unsanitary conditions often for long periods of time, facilitating the transmission of infectious diseases among and between species, and then spreading to the humans with whom they come in contact.
data.result_and_outcome:
With our assistance and training, two Peruvian communities previously involved in illegal trade now have registered tourism associations. These associations democratically allocate the revenue gained from low-impact nature tourism activities for services and infrastructures that benefit the whole community and local ecosystem.
Thanks to the collaboration with online promoters and a nearby reserve, the communities now receive tourists full time, providing a salary for 60 people, improving family income from 15% - 42%. This tourism income further incentivises the sustainable management of their natural resources.
data.description_of_solution: Implement sustainable low-impact, nature tourism initiatives in indigenous communities to reduce natural resource extraction.
data.org_mission: A grassroots NGO dedicated to conserving biodiversity and improving local livelihoods in the Amazonian border area between Colombia, Brazil, and Peru.
data.activities: Since 2010, Entropika has worked with key communities previously involved in illegal natural resource extraction to develop sustainable economic alternatives such as low-impact Wildlife Watching Tourism (WWT) and experiential tourism initiatives.
data.impact_numbers: Tourism providing salary for 60 people for two Peruvian communities previously involved in illegal trade now have registered tourism associations
data.lessons_learned:
Challenges when working with rural or indigenous communities include Illiteracy, gender inequality, illegal activities, corruption, difficult to reach areas, and continuous rotation of local authorities hinder the implementation of long-term conservation processes.  For example, in our community tourism project, association members struggled with organization and accounting, making it difficult to keep track of visitors and incoming revenue. 
Recruit young members of local families is a crucial step for sustaining competencies, vibrancy, and longevity of the projects. 
Execute continuous training and capacity building because people forget quickly. Repetition helps people recall previously acquired knowledge and maintain a good quality service to bring more satisfied customers.   
Identify and mobilize local leaders. They empower indigenous communities to manage their own economic activities.  The communities we support that have strong leadership have made greater strides and advances in implementing the nature tourism program than those with weak political systems. 
Transferring skills among communities. Our capacity-building strategy involves formal and informal leaders from more advanced projects training and transferring skills to other communities so that they can replicate those experiences.  
Promote multiple money-making initiatives. As the pandemic demonstrated, communities who have relied on one economic alternative, such as tourism, struggle with food security. Ecosystem services like farming crops can be used to prepare traditional food products for sale or trade. Keeping local traditions is critical for the long-term survival of rural communities.

data.title: Strengthening law enforcement capacities to combat wildlife trafficking
data.region: The tri-border Amazon region of Colombia, Brazil, and Peru
data.problem_statement: The trafficking of wildlife for use in tourist attractions poses an ongoing risk to wild populations of animals, especially primates, throughout South America. Entropika focuses on halting the illegal wildlife trade driven by wildlife encounter tourism across the Colombian-Peruvian Amazon border. Captive wild animals used in tourism attractions have frequent direct contact with people who feed them and take photos with them, posing high zoonotic risks for humans and animals alike.
data.result_and_outcome:
Five Peruvian communities that feature wildlife for tourism were visited. Species, approximate age, and health conditions of birds, primates, rodents, and reptiles in exhibition were recorded and photographic records were taken.
Sixty-five representatives in law enforcement from five countries (Colombia, Brazil, Peru, Chile, and the US) participated in the capacity-building workshop.
Entropika organized two wildlife confiscation operations with Iquitos authorities carried out in Peru, recovering a total of 34 live animals, including endangered species, and multiple animal derivatives. Animals were transported by two hydroplanes to rescue and rehab centers in Iquitos. 
These operations eliminated the majority of wildlife selfie tourism operations in the region, and set a precedent for improved law enforcement in the tri-border area.
data.description_of_solution:
Quantify the incidence of wildlife trafficking for tourism in Peruvian communities.  
Train local authorities to take coordinated actions to confiscate timber and wildlife through a capacity-building workshop for law enforcement officials from the Amazon triple border region of Brazil, Peru, and Colombia. Entropika and the US Fish and Wildlife Service organized the workshop to strengthen institutional capacities and improve interagency collaboration to effectively apprehend wildlife poachers, seize environmental contraband, and deliver confiscated animals to approved rescue facilities. An addition, environmental prosecutors officers were taken to Peruvian communities to see examples of wildlife trade promoted by tourism.
The prosecutor’s office from Iquitos, Peru requested Entropika's support in executing a confiscation operation in one of the Peruvian communities where Entropika had previously documented the exploitation of wildlife as photo props for tourists.
data.org_mission: A grassroots NGO dedicated to conserving biodiversity and improving local livelihoods in the Amazonian border area between Colombia, Brazil, and Peru.
data.impact_numbers: Tri-border workshop conducted
data.lessons_learned:
Use discretion concerning exposure of your name linked to police intervention of organized crime. The media coverage of Entropika's involvement in the police seizure of wild animals used for selfie tourism in Peru angered tourism agencies (and the mafioso families behind them) who sought retaliation over the loss of their cash cow. A day after a National Geographic article was published featuring their role in the operation, Entropika's director received a death threat targeting her and her team via e-mail. For the second operation, Entropika kept a low profile in order to avoid association with the confiscation. 
If you receive a death threat it is important to inform all law enforcement authorities including upper levels of central governments since local authorities are often bribed and will not take the appropriate measures to safeguard environmental defenders’ lives.

data.title: Environmental Litigation to Stop Night Monkey Trafficking for Biomedical Research
data.region: The tri-border Amazon region of Colombia, Brazil, and Peru
data.support_needed:
We could use support in areas where we lack expertise, for instance, digital fluency in software programs, design programs, and media tools, mainly due to our geographical isolation in an area with slow internet connectivity. Being a part of this alliance also affords us the opportunity to make connections with likeminded organizations and individuals to join efforts in mutually beneficial research proposals and conservation endeavors. Likewise, we would like to improve/strengthen our law enforcement actions at the triple border area between Colombia-Brazil-Peru because we experience high levels of WLT and regional corruption. 
Furthermore, receiving assistance from the experts in EndPandemics in reviewing our funding proposals and publications before submission would be hugely beneficial for us. Also, we are involved in various law cases to protect biodiversity and expose corruption, and we often need signatures from colleagues, academics, and conservation groups for our petitions to the Colombian government. Thus, support from EndPandemics would be great for future appeals.
data.problem_statement:
At the Colombian-Peruvian border of the Amazon, wild night monkeys are harvested for malaria research by a single Colombian biomedical laboratory that illegally sources 70% of their test subjects from Peruvian communities. The continuous extraction of night monkeys decimates local primate populations and contributes to the deforestation of the Amazon since wide expanses of trees are felled during the capture process. 
After experimentation, trafficked night monkeys are released back into the wild without screening for diseases or assessment on how resident populations are affected by the influx of released animals. 
Night monkeys are susceptible to human pathogens such as TB and herpes simplex virus, and releasing them after prolonged captivity, especially immunocompromised, could introduce harmful diseases into wild populations or establish sylvatic cycles of disease with the potential for spillback from animals to humans.
Entropika takes legal action to stop the trade of night monkeys and the exploitation of indigenous trappers.
data.result_and_outcome:
In 2014, Entropika's director won the lawsuit, and trapping permits for night monkeys were revoked until 2016. This ruling stopped the capture of approximately 4,000 monkeys per year and reduced the risk of endemic disease transmission from primates to indigenous trappers.
National and international media coverage of the landmark case exposed corruption, unethical research, and environmental damages costing the laboratory financial backing and prestige. 
In 2017, Nancy Ma's night monkey was upgraded from Least Concern to Vulnerable on IUCN's Red List. 
In 2019, at Entropika's request, the Comptroller General ordered disciplinary and penal investigations against Corpoamazonia, the regional environmental authority, and the Ministry of Environment, marking the first time that criminal investigations will be carried out regarding the illegal trade in night monkeys. 
Entropika is currently contesting the lab’s latest permits to extract 400 monkeys a year from indigenous territories for the period 2020-2022 in court.
data.description_of_solution:
In 2011, Entropika’s director filed a “popular benefit” lawsuit, setting off a series of ongoing legal battles to protect night monkey populations from wildlife trafficking for vaccine research. 
Entropika uses the court system to hold Colombian national and regional environmental authorities and the biomedical facility accountable for corruption, negligence in issuing permits, unregulated post-experimental releases, and exceeding legal trapping quotas by procuring trafficked monkeys from Peru.
data.org_mission: A grassroots NGO dedicated to conserving biodiversity and improving local livelihoods in the Amazonian border area between Colombia, Brazil, and Peru.
data.activities: We can provide Information from the frontline and specific case studies demonstrating why the End Pandemics stance against wildlife trade is important in a real-world context and lend research/data for End Pandemics objectives. We can also share our experience and expertise in webinar series or other media outlets (if internet connection allows this).
data.impact_numbers: Conducted census fieldwork in several indigenous communities, private reserves, and state-owned land to estimate the status of wildlife populations
data.lessons_learned:
Perseverance, adaptability, and continuous follow-up are the key lessons when entering into litigation. Despite several setbacks with the judicial system, public servants will finally be investigated for corruption, making it more difficult for the biomedical facility to obtain trapping permits in the future. 
Main obstacles faced are the sluggishness of the court system. Powerful environmental offenders can bribe court officers who will seek any oversight to throw out a case, such as not responding in time to a hearing appointment. Legal teams will utilize obstruction and delay tactics to waste time and resources. In Entropika’s case, the defense has repeatedly rescheduled court hearings, causing money to be lost in lawyer fees, flight tickets, and lodging. In addition, Entropika’s director became the target of a strategic lawsuit against public participation (SLAPP) by the lab’s director to silence claims of wrongdoing by draining financial resources, time, and emotional energy. 
In retrospect, paying for representation from a strong law firm from the start would aid in advancing legal processes and save time and energy. However, the resources available only allow for the services of a low-cost lawyer with limited experience, leaving Entropika to shoulder most of the legal work. 
Advice to other organizations is to be prepared to face intimidation tactics such as SLAPPs and secure sufficient funds for unexpected expenses and a drawn-out legal process.

data.title: Establishing an Electronic Monitoring System for Legal Wildlife Trade
data.problem_statement: This project was initiated by two Australian charities, For the Love of Wildlife and Nature Needs More in order to modernise the CITES system of monitoring legal wildlife trade through a paper-based system that has not been updated since 1975.
data.result_and_outcome: So far, only one country has adopted the eCITES BaseSolution.  The system includes species names, appendix listings, units and classifications and can be centrally updated ensuring consistency in global electronic permit exchange. Several countries have adopted their own digital systems which are inoperable with the eCITES system and and do not offer the same level of security. Modernising the legal trade permit and management system will make supply chains more transparent, and will help to address biosecurity risks inherent in any trade in wildlife.
data.description_of_solution: A fully digital system called eCITES BaseSolution was developed by UNCTAD and CITES with support from the Swiss and Sri Lankan governments. It was rolled out  in Sri Lanka in late 2019 and to date no other country has adopted it.  The cost is $150k per country or $30 million for all 183 signatories to CITES.

data.title: Media Campaign to Eliminate Commercial Trade in Wild Animals and Introduce One Health Policy
data.country: Thailand, India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, West Africa, Brazil
data.problem_statement: An overwhelming majority of the world remains unaware how large and detrimental the business of commercial trade in wild animals is, not only to the animals, but also to people due to the risk of zoonotic outbreaks.  Those who may have some level of awareness may not know that the legal trade in wild animals is equally capable of transmitting zoonotic diseases as illegally traded animals.  The viruses do not discriminate.  Furthermore, much of the public and government decision makers (not to mention senior level inter-governmental bodies) may mistakenly think that a ban on commercial trade in wild animals means banning subsistence hunting (commercial and subsistence are by definition vastly different).
data.result_and_outcome: Over 100 stories placed in at least 10 languages in every market in the world, reaching at least 700 million people.
data.description_of_solution: To tell the convenient truth: that the recurrence and severity of pandemics can be drastically reduced through the strokes of pens by lawmakers who have it in their power to ban commercial trade in wild animals.  And to clarify what such bans would look like (for example, that they would not include a ban on subsistence hunting).  This campaign clearly illuminates the connection between wildlife poaching and trade to zoonotic outbreaks.  Animals that are taken from, or pushed out of their natural environments, can carry a pathogen with them into human populations which have no immune response to that pathogen.  This message is delivered via newsprint stories, TV stories, Opinion Editorials, and social media.

They want to be frontline so they can verify the information and experience what you are talking about.  They became journalists in part for their hunger for facts and adventure.  4. data.country: Kenya, South Africa, Thailand, Vietnam,  China, Turkey, Laos

Staff working for airlines and airports, freight forwarders and seaports, as well as banks, hotels, and other companies are participating in Freeland training and awareness programs that create trafficking free zones. What works: 1. Keep the training and meetings short and simple.  Work around the schedules of your target audience (they are busy and usually can only spare half-day). 2. Minimize controls of large donor agencies and large conservation organizations that can bring heavy restrictions and conditions that slow the process down, and/or make the trainings too long or academic. data.title: C-TOC (Counter Transnational Organized Crime)
data.country: Kenya, Uganda, Congo Brazzaville, Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, Thailand, Malaysia, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam, China, India, Brazil
data.problem_statement: Criminal rings and syndicates targeting wild animals and their habitats for commercial sale operate across provincial/state and national borders to move the stolen "goods" to from source to buyer.  This means that their illicit supply chains cross multiple agency and national jurisdictions.  However, most agencies and countries do not share data on these illicit supply chains because they do not know they have data or access to data that can fill an important part of a criminal investigation puzzle.  Or they are not empowered to share that data across agency or national lines.
data.result_and_outcome:
1. Freeland delivered CTOC training course to African and Asian enforcement officers, including the use of i2.  Utilizing new data and new link analysis skills, the officers tracked down and arrested 5 men (3 Nigerians, 1 Congolese, and 1 Chinese) who are part of a major cross-continental syndicate that has been sponsoring the killing of thousands of elephants and pangolins for years.  
2. CTOC-trained officers have opened a cross-border money laundering and racketeering case against a syndicate whose criminal activities straddle 9 countries.
data.description_of_solution: C-TOC convenes and empowers enforcement agencies to illuminate, analyze, and disrupt illicit supply chains involved in trafficking.   Agencies and trusted officers straddling the illicit supply chain are selected and brought together to form an enforcement chain, and are trained using conventional and AI and ML techniques.
data.org_mission: Protect vulnerable wild animals, communities and ecosystems from trafficking and over-exploitation.  Our Vision is a world of pristine ecosystems that is free of wildlife trafficking and human slavery
data.impact_numbers: More than 500 officers trained in CTOC globally
data.lessons_learned: 1. Some donors and governments place heavy bureaucratic restrictions on international enforcement meetings, including lengthy vetting processes.  2. Governments will send the wrong people to enforcement gatherings unless they are carefully selected through precise TORs.  3. Supervisors or senior officers of the enforcement agencies must be included in the process, or else the officer who has been trained or equipped with new information may not be enabled to put his/her benefits to use once back home. 4. NGOs should be given a space at CTOCs to present their insights, and then can be asked to leave the room once sensitive law enforcement discussions take place.
